New Orleans.

November the 8th, 9th. Born 1908. November the 9th, 1908. The 60th or 70th of November.

No, classical. Trickling class?

The reason why I don't know, because when I was born, she had gave that up. Oh, I see. Because she gave me that violin when I got around about 10 years old. She gave it to me. Did you play anything? Banjo.
Banjo before violin. That's right.

No, yeah, banjo before violin. That's right. I took up banjo in 1925. About a year and a half later, I went to work with Paul Moody. You might have heard of Paul Moody. I worked with his band for quite a while. Then I decided I wanted to take up sax. I took lessons from Professor David Jones on the Pelican. He used to be an old Pelican Rampart and Grabby. Then I began to play a little bit. Then I went to work playing sax. The Paul Moody band. Then from there, I went to the quarters. I stayed in the quarters for many years. I worked at a joint called the Last Ronda. On a gamble between Dolphin and whoever. Last Ronda. I must have worked there about six years, six or seven years ago.
What time did it close?
We used to go to work at 10, knock off at 5, 6, 7 o'clock in the morning. Wasn't making what a dollar a night. Plus Tips.
Well, it was a good name for the joint. Yeah, it was a good joint. We made it pretty good.
Our Tips used to be four or five dollars a night apiece. We had a piece, Tips. We made it over.
That's for the whole band or a piece? A piece.

The Tips was great. The salaries wasn't them, but the Tips was great. Then after I went with Tips Howard then, I stayed with him for a long while. Then I left. I went on the road with Dan Moody's band out of Buccaloosa. We traveled all over Tennessee, Louisiana, Mississippi. I stayed with him about three years. I came back. I went back with Kit Howard. I worked with Kit Howard about two years. Then I went with George Williams. I stayed with George Williams a long time. Then after George went to work at the Peddorf, he turned the big band over to me, but I gave it up because it was too much of a headache. The flaws didn't show up and come late. So I let that go and I went to work at Pepper's. You saw him out there at Pepper's, 327 Boydman Street with Pickle out there. That's where I worked for a long time out there. Peppers? Peppers, yeah. Peppers, yeah. 327 Boydman Street. And I was there a little while. Then after that, pulled up. Well, I did spot jobs. Ways in different little clubs out there. Wow. Then doing up the spot jobs after that. Then we were hitting a few chips with Al. We came back but I was spotting around and playing different groups. Until I met my good friend. I went with him. Yeah, well that day at downtown, that's the one at Toulouse and Bourbon or? Toulouse and Bourbon.
The motel there? Yeah. Yeah.

We made those with him. As long as I was living back on the lakefront, up on Joe something, we went to his house and recorded those records. Right. His house one Sunday. So, this by, by our best by having a pretty good deal, we caught on to the right. Wasn't a trouble at all. But I didn't know none of the numbers because I had never worked rehearsals with, you know. Just quick set up, record those records.

No, I hadn't been working with Dave. Yeah, I see. All at once he wanted to record his records. That was his own numbers he wanted to record. So, I went on back there and we made them.
Well, they're pretty standard New Orleans numbers. The changes are pretty much the same.
Well, some of them were his own ideas. Really good.
Yeah, but I was trying to imagine some of them. Same old changes like the Bucket changes, but different melodies.
That's right. It seems to me.
I don't know. I just fooled around with them a little bit, but I can play them. Let's see. You knew old man Jim Humphreys, you said, huh?

The old man. Yeah, the old man. The Willie Graham. The old man. Yeah. The old man. Yeah. They lived on Clow or Willow Street, between Janet and Cadiz. They used to go there and take my lessons. I was going to school then, but I was going to take my lessons. Where I went. Up around Cadiz and Liberty I think. Oh yeah. Yeah.
It was on Liberty between Janet and Cadiz. I used to go there twice a week out of school. Take my lessons.

What part of town were you brought up in? Up in the 12th Ward. Well I was born on this one. I was raised up in the Irish Channel. Do you know where you were born exactly? On St. Anthony. St. Anthony. Somewhere in the South. I was born in the South. I was born in the South. I was born in the South.
What part of town were you brought up in?
Up in the 12th Ward, up around the Irish Channel. Well, I was born around this one. I was raised up in the Irish Channel.
Do you know where you were born exactly?
On St. Anthony. St. Anthony, between Durden and Claiborne. I don't know the number of the houses. I think somewhere around where Sidney Peace was staying.
Do you remember anything from that day, right?

No, because I was a baby. See, my mom and my dad separated. And before my daddy had me, I went to live with my uncle up on Laura Street. On Laura and 39th block of Laura, and that's where I was raised up there.
Around Constantinople, I know that.

Yeah, but it's between General Taylor and Austin. That's where I was raised. And after I got married, I stayed up there a while. But I wanted to come back down where I was born. I'd come back down here.
So you weren't too terribly far from the Humber's house? No, I wasn't too far from that. You could walk there if you had to walk back.

That's right. I could walk back. I lived more and after we moved off to Constantinople, I lived more and general Taylor's. Right where that was right around the corner. I wasn't too far away. And what about the banjo? How did you learn the banjo? Well, I have a few ideas. I had a friend of mine, Nathaniel Morris. He was a great banjoist. Who? Nathaniel Morris. He has a son that's great, two sons, at least great drummers. One of them they call, what that boy, I can't call his name. He's up in St. Louisville. He's up in St. Louis now. Well, he was a good musician. And I used to go to him and take lessons from him. Well, I have a few ideas about it because I used to play ukulele. I had good ideas about it. So I took lessons from him for a while. Then Kimmel used to come out and back from my house and sit out there and give me ideas and all that too. Well, what sort of ideas would they give you? Well, just showing your dick and finger in the higher bill cards and all that too. You know? Huh? You studied comedy then, some? Yeah. On your own? On my own, yeah. On my own. Yeah, I studied on my own. Well, I knew music already. But all I had to learn was the fingers. And David Jones would tell me all the time, you go home, you practice your music. But forget about it. Put it aside. Knowing out of your head. Knowing how you call it, just out of your head. And that's what I do. But I was going to take lessons during the same time. Manuel Sells was playing with the band with David Jones, but he was taking lessons too. Sam there as I was there, he would be there. But he was already playing with that orchestra. That was a rest of the band. He was working with the band. I was playing with the band. I was playing with the band. I was playing with the band. I was playing with the band.
How did you really get into playing? Was it mainly through the lessons? Did you work out some of your own ideas? How do you do that?

Well, I have a lot of ideas. I don't try, if I can't help it, from trying to follow behind some other guys. I try to work my own way, but everybody say now, it seems like I'm copying behind Charlie Parker, which I think. But I don't play style on Charlie Parker, but I try to play. I like to play music, but I like to play in a certain swing, a certain way. You see? I got ideas. I use my own ideas at times.
Well, who did you like? Who did you listen to when you were coming out? Different issues.
Well, my idol on saxophone was the great guy that died with Duke. John Hopkins. That's the kind of style of sax I love.
Well, you know who his favorite was? Who? My favorite was Bechet. Oh, yeah, yeah. He loved Bechet. I don't see New Orleans.

Yeah, you never did know him though, huh? Bechet? Yeah. No, Cindy Bechet. Yeah. No, I think he left there before I even got a teenager. I guess. Yeah. Well, you knew his brother, I guess. Yeah. Leonard. Yeah, I knew his brother. Yeah, I knew his brother. Just like Big O, I didn't know about him, but I knew his brother. Yeah. Some guys left me all before I was up in my teens.
Well, who did you hear when you were coming up though, I mean, before Hodges? You must have heard some different people when you were a kid here.
Well, we had like old Fess. I can't think of him. He's a New Orleans born too. He was playing with Count. We call him Fess. He died a while back.
What did he play?
Tenor sax. Oh, I can't say.
Was he before Lester Young or after Lester Young?
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

I took ukulele when I was just coming about 22, 23 years old. Then in 1925, that's when I was born in the first band.
In 1925, you were much first band. And then when did you stay to fiddle?
Well, that was when I was going to school. I was about 10, between 10 and 11 years old.
And you started the saxophone that time?
Why were you playing when the Depression hit, when it started?
Last Ronda. I guess you remember that. Yeah, last Ronda.
And what instrument were you playing then?

I was playing sax. You were playing sax? I had Albert Walter who was on trumpet. Joe Paris. Either Alton Cornel. Alton Cornel was a voicemail. And he left and we got Joe Paris. And we had Albert Giles on the drums. And Katsun, he was a band with him. One-eyed babes.
Yeah, that's correct.
That's correct.
Joe Phillips or whatever. Yeah, Babe Phillips.
I played some jobs with him, but he's a comical man. Yeah, he couldn't speak English out of him. No, you couldn't understand him. That's right.
Where did you get that vega banjo?

Uh, he probably gave it to one of us. Oh, John Bernard gave it to one of us? That's right. One of the time, him and some other people came. I played a parade with John and they walked up and asked me, said, we went to two of the great banjo. I said, I did. He said, would you want one to come back? I said, yeah, I'll tell you. I thought he was joking. Went by his house and picked up the banjo. I said, I'm a father out there. But the trouble is, they got a ring. Now you can't get a break on a banjo. If you're not in that ring out there on Boyle Street, you can't get a job.
Oh no, you have to be in the city.
That's right, you got to be in that ring out there.
You got to belong to that ring. Yeah, well you could double. That's true. You can play two instruments, you should have it made. But you've got to get in.
That's right.
When was the first time you ever saw anybody with a sax? Do you remember?

Yeah, of course I played with the first guy I know was playing alto was Peter Bailey. His son is a bass player now. Chuck. Chuck. His daddy was playing in the same band that I was with Moje. Then we had another guy, he was an Alabama alto player too, Edmund Washington. Big fat dude. Those two who worked in the band were. I haven't seen him watch in a long time. He lived uptown in some way. Yeah. I'd see him up around Carrollton and play when I ran into him on the street. He didn't even know me.
That's the guy who gave me a kind of encouragement. Because Pete used to tell him all the time, oh man, you'll never make a saxophone player.

You'll just hear to see me get on that instrument. And the voice to tell him all the time, go ahead and sound nice. But Washington would tell me all the time, go ahead, you sound nice. And well, when doing rehearsal with the band, I'd take my own with the band, play numbers with the band. So after a while, they got rid of Pete, and they put me in the band, alto.

Alto.
Two altos?
Two altos, yeah. Two altos.
Did you have a tenor?

No, I wouldn't attend the band. We'd be in two altos. Oh, I had Moehead's son was playing Clienthead on his motorboat. His first name was Raymond, but I can't tell you that Spanish name he had. He was from Delacroix, somewhere around there.
They got so many names, Nunez and Malaria and Garcia, you can't remember Mariah. That's right.
That's right. That's right. I worked with them on Goodwild. We used to go around Delacroix, you know.

The trumpet. The trumpet player.

Paul Moehead.
Paul. And his son's name was Paul too?

Yeah.

I think I was in the quarters. I think I was in the quarters. I think I was in the quarters of World War II. Uh, it wasn't that the last round, though.
You were there a long time?

The Club Arlington?

Arlington. Right where, uh, Woolworth's now on Ramp on Canal. Uh-huh. Right in the middle of the block they had a club they called, uh, Club Arlington. And I worked there. Oh, Arlington. Arlington. I worked there six months with them. Bill and D.D. and Alba Jow.

Mm-hm. Decatur Street was Boorman Street. Mm-hm. Boorman Street wasn't no one. Yeah. It wasn't nothing. Decatur Street was everything. All the club was right there on Decatur Street.

Wilming Street wasn't on it. Wasn't nothing. Wasn't a thing on Wilming Street. Decairn Street was everything. All the clubs was right there on Decairn Street. But it was rough. It was a rough place to go on Decairn Street.
They didn't have any fights or anything?

Yeah. During that time, those Chong brothers, you might have heard of them Ralph Chong and a whole bunch of them out there. They used to go to clubs picking fights and all those people out there. But things was reasonable. Of course the money wasn't good. Wasn't making no money out there. I tell these young musicians, man, we wait for 75 cents a night. They don't believe me. 75 cents. I'll never forget one night, Leon Primer, Louis Primer's brother, came in the last round of and he said, and he let me play. So he went to the boss. He said, you got a minor fine saxophone player back then. So when Leon left, he called me. He said, come here. He said, I'm going to give you a raise. He called me a raise. He called me a raise. He called me a raise.
That was a big buck.

And I had a white fellow. He was a county. He was waking. Oh, at 1 and close. And he stopped by and asked me to come and give his wife some idea. And he never forget that back in Bucktown. He used to go back there twice a week and give her ideas on the album. So sexy. She could read, but she couldn't execute on it. And that was the main thing he wanted me to do. So I used to go back there twice a week and give her a few lessons and whatnot.
Could you get off at all, play by hand?
Huh?
Could she play by hand?

That's what she couldn't do. That's what she said. Oh, and that's what you were showing her. Yeah, that's what I was showing her. She was a pretty good musician. But she couldn't execute on it. She was like, you know, like I was doing something like that. So I'd go there. I would write a little fingering down for her, you know what I'm saying? Wake it out and she seemed to be good. She was doing pretty good. But after I started working regularly, I couldn't go back there anymore. And I haven't seen her in a couple of things.
I don't know. I don't know. How many women saxathons played her?
Well, I don't think she wanted to work on the band. She just wanted to be around home with, you know. She was piano player, so I guess she enjoyed being together playing like a chick.
Well, they had the Sweet Hearts of Rhythm.
Oh yeah. And then they had that other girl. Peg or somebody had a band. Because they came out to the Orphering Theater lots of times. All girls band. They were really good.

How old were you when he was alive today?
He had been about six to seven. I've been around my place. 67. Yeah, you've been here.

That's funny that I never ran across him, but I guess, see I've only been here 26 years now. 26 years? I guess I've known you since I was 25. Something like that. As soon as I started following the brass bands.
It don't seem like that long, those times. No.

Well, maybe I didn't know you when I first came around, you know. I didn't know everybody in the bands. I would just follow them. I'd get to know people like Left Hand Buster and so forth. He was one of my favorite trombone players.

Buster, yeah.
Left Hand Buster. Yeah, he was just playing with us.

Yeah. Yeah. I remember Bunk Johnson. Yeah.
I remember Bunk Johnson. Yeah. Yeah. I remember Bunk Johnson.

Bunk Johnson had another nice trombone player, Maurice Duran. He was a nice trombone player. Who did he play? He was away from me a long time too. He came back and I think he did some work with Sidney Duran after he came back here.
Did you ever work with Sidney Duran? I did. I did. I did.
I was awake there. Did you ever work up at the Tulane Alumni House on Willow Street? Yeah, I certainly did. on the Saturday. We were there on a Friday evening. I sure did.
I worked there on a Friday. Well they didn't drink up there. Did you? They sure didn't drink up there.

They sure didn't drink up there. No lick at all. the afternoon and play before the football game like the football game was a Saturday. We were there on a Friday evening. I sure did. I worked there on a Friday. Well they didn't drink up there. They sure didn't. They sure didn't drink up there. No liquor at all. I think I played that one time and they had liquor. One time. One time I think. One time? I think so. One time they would get some liquor in. But otherwise, other times we'd have liquor.

You don't like the maple there? No. I used to carry two glasses at once in case I ran out. They really wore it on. They had a good time. Yeah, it was nice. They always liked Joyce. Yeah, they did. Everybody liked Joyce. I don't see how you worked. I mean, that man. How many jobs would he play? And work?
He was working at the theater. When he'd get off from the theater, he would go to the wax museum, work there. Then go play music all night. And then play a parade?
And play a parade, that's right. Yeah. Can you imagine? That's right.
Three and four jobs. That's right. That's right. And he still find time to get in trouble, I mean. Find time to go around all them women's he had. Oh, that man was so good.

He used to tell me about all the different places he'd be at home. You know, I mean, just for kicks, he'd be going around all these places. That's right. And yet I knew he'd be working three jobs. I couldn't see how he could work in the paddock, and clean up the theaters, and clean up the wax museum, and still have time for all that fun.

That's right. He sure did. He sure did. When did he sleep? Sure again, the- He got about an hour or so sleep with him. That's what his boss told me. I played for them at Prince Coni. I went out and he said, he used to tell George all the time, he's doing too much work. He said, George, your in-laws, haunt. Who told you that? Mr. Lazarus. Oh, yeah. And he said that he told George to quit doing all that work. If he needed that money, call him to him. He would help his mom, he said, doing all that work. Say, all right, come and clean up the show in the morning. Then go home and go to rest. Then go to work at night. All that wax museum and all that. What George said, George, he had his heart. He wouldn't do it.
He'd have his little grandson, a great-grandson or something. Yeah, little grandson, yeah. His grandson, I remember that.

You know that boy got killed. No, I didn't know that. Yeah, he was a drummer, you know. And some woman shot him in Texas. About two years ago. He was a nice drummer. The little lady killed me. Yeah, George, sure. George was something one time. He was a kickster. But he was a good drummer, though. A good drummer and a good bass drum player, too. I'll never forget what John Casimir had in his band. Knox was out the union, and Knox couldn't play with nothing. So George said, I'm tired of playing this bass drum. I'm going to get Knox. So he went and put Knox in the union. Put Knox back in the union to get Knox to play in the band.
Well this was after Steve died, because you wouldn't remember this.
Snoop the Russell's part of the band. Yeah.

Snoop the Russell's part of the band. Yeah. But Steve Ingram died. And whenever John Casimir had a job, he would have joined George Williams on bass drum. And when George Williams had a job, he'd have John on the band. That's right. So they had it work out where it was all the same.
All the same band, that's right. Just about. That's right. That's who he was.
They were cleaning up. They were double dipping. That's right. I guess I could just change the cap. That's all. Just change the cap. That's all. All right. Oh, well, you know.
Just like the Eureka band, they were using the bands out of every band, all of Brad's bands. They didn't have too many bands left out of that band.
What happened to the Eureka? Anything?
Well, all of them died. Yeah. Only one, I think two of them lived, that's Poissy and Magnapol.
Well, Magnapol quit them before.
Yeah, he did quit. But then, yeah. But all the rest of them died.
Just about everybody in the band. She was with them. Yeah, she was with them. After Richardson left.
That's right.
And Richardson's got out of the union for a week. So that's about it. Right. At least the old one.
Well, is Magnapol still with the old happy band? Yeah, he's still with them. Because I worked with them the week before that, at the Roseville Hotel. Well, half the town they have two jobs.
Yeah, well, they'll have different guys from the Tuxedo. They use Knox and Trotta.
Yeah, because the job I played Knox and Trotta was with Harold on, the other job at the Marriott. And I was like, I do a lot of work with them. They get me working with them too.
Getting all the work through that time. It turns out, huh?
Yeah, they were working three hours in one day, four jobs in one day, a week ago. So they made me money.

Well, I can remember one week when I had, when they had, I think, four funerals in a row. Four days, they'd have funerals. And they didn't play funerals on Sunday because the drivers charged more. Yeah. They were numbers in the drafts. They charged overtime for working on Sundays.
I don't think the graves deal, they don't open cemeteries on Sunday. They might not be. Well, that's the rules, no funerals on Sunday.
Yeah.
The only funerals they have is the Jewish, you know. But they would have a lot of work for the Brazilians.

And a lot of work with some of the churches too. Right. That's right. Different church associations, aren't they? That's right. I know I believe in men and women for churches. So was it the ideal of doing these divorce? Yeah.
Yeah. I know I believe in men and women for churches. Was it the ideal of doing these divorce?
Square deal. Square deal.
Square deal. Yeah. That was a good parade.
That sure was. Square deal was right. What was the longest parade you ever played? I'm going to tell you the longest parade I was playing was last corner up in Metro.
Yeah, up in Metro. Yeah, up in Metro.
Yeah, up in Metro.

Jefferson Pass with Bryant. That's the longest parade, the hardest parade I played all my whole career. The hours were short but you walk, they walk the devil like this. It's not like these close dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear You gotta stop there, stop there. You walk without a stop. All true, Kevin. Never no more. Never more.
That's with Brian? Yeah, with Brian.

The young trumpet player? Yeah. That's right. So I said, never no more. I had a job sitting out. Why didn't he bring Joe Gordon out to a parade? I'd rather stay in New Orleans and play a car with the parade, and go out there and play. Because you do get some kind of a parade to rest. Something to eat, something to drink. Out there, you're gonna get nothing. That's a lot of things.
Do you know that club they call the Buzzards?

I wait for them. I wait for Buzzards. That's all George used to wait for, Buzzards. Then after he left the Buzzards, went to wait for the Lions Club. Of course we used to wait for the El Norah Club. We used to even play the Dancers on Saturday night. But the best club in the city to work for is the Commerce Club. That's the best. The Commerce. The which? Commerce Club from the Garden District. Around Washington? Yeah, starting around Thurid and Chippewa, I think. Called the Connors. That's the best club. You don't do all that walking. They don't. When they leave from Thurid and Chippewa, they go to the part of the region in Annapolis, and they go back and they come on out to Canal Street. Then they come around, and they got buses waiting for you. They take you up to Jefferson Avenue. Then you get off there and you walk, ride the chopper too, to speak. You got a big place there where you go to your hot meal. Then from there you walk on downtown, or they walk like the Mother Club, circling all over the city. Even from Northern Park, Orr-Morke Park, walk to Canal Street, walk back up to Arrheny. I used to do that.

I used to run from one club to the other. I'd follow the lines, the buses from Hardin Park, and then I'd run and catch the Corner Club, and then run and catch the Yellow Jays, and then catch the Garden District.
Sometimes we had a car.
There were a lot of those clubs.
That's right.
I don't know how many of them are going there.
They're all of them going. You still got all those clubs. They're all over them. I don't think you'll see much more of the lines club because last time my parade for them,
remember Andrew?
They didn't have many members. When they got to Canal Street and started back up, if they had 15 members, they had 100, because they had nobody left for the parade.
I can't figure that out. You know, Jerry, I forget his last name, the captain was there.
Jerry Alamond. He wasn't there.
I can't think of the different guy's name.
One guy.
Yes.
Ronnie West. I didn't see him. We called him Red. I don't know if Red wasn't there either. We called him Red.

Buddy was there. Now Buddy is about 75 or 80 years old. I think he'd been marching for something like 55 years in the streets or more. I think he was the only person who was ever Grand Marshall's wives or something like that. Anyway, I don't see the regular members when I go. Oh no. And they used to come to Munster's too. And I don't see them there. I don't know what happened. They must have fallen out with Munster herself.
They've got a club down the street, the place they all go to. That could be it.
Where's Munster's at? Lions and Laurel.
That's right there by the playground where you started.
Oh yeah, that's right, but they got their own players now. We used to go down the street.
Not Brits?
No. I don't know what they're doing. Annunciation and lines?
A line between Annunciation and Chapitua. It's a place that they built. Oh, they built them on. That explains a lot. Yeah, they got their own club out there. Well, maybe that's why they went to town.
Yeah. Well, that's the place Tony was playing at, Munster.

That's where Munster? Yeah, Tony was playing. I thought Munster was in Calvary's Bar someway. No, no. Well, that's Munster. Yeah, well, you know it. Right by the ballpark. Yeah. I thought Munster was in Calvary's Bar someway. No, no. That's Munster.
Yeah, well, you know it.

Right by the ballpark. Yeah. Well, I have told Tony and them talking about Munster. I thought it was up in Campison somewhere. I didn't know where that was Munster. I always thought that was the Lions Club. They own that club. Yeah.

Well, that's right by home plate there. Yeah. Where you used to go and meet. Right. So many different guys I want to ask you about. You never did tell me much about Billy and the Dee and John. Well, I can tell you they were pretty nice fellas, people to work with.

They were pretty good to work with. And we worked together quite a long while. All they told us was during that time. They both used to fight the battle and it was all the trouble with them. Of course, he was the cause of us to lose the job out there by the club out there. He had a cross here with a trumpet. Busts of heads. We lost the job there. Hmm. You had a bus of trumpet?
No, you hear it with the bell. The edge of the bell.

And this guy, you say, the boss, he comes to and says, what happened Billy? Oh, when I was coming to work, I fell off the streetcar. He said, no, you're lying. I said, because I was looking at you when you were coming here. There wasn't nothing wrong with you with me. I was being brought with me, gushing out of him. So he said, suppose they could suspend him for two weeks. Give him two weeks suspension. We went with our golf. Told the waiters to come back there. Tell us don't come back no more. We all lost the job. That boy was tough, rough doing that time. Do you know what I mean? But outside of that, they were pretty good people who were good. Pretty good. And so funny how they just went up to the world, just take me up. When we was in St. Louis, that's where we met when we were going to Mexico. They met us in St. Louis. They walked around there. East one of them got $6,000 tied around here. They wasted $6,000 in trust in the bank. Folks, I had been doing DD for years, man. Both of them. In fact, I've been building with them, working on Charles and Dekayla and Dumaine. That was your top-notch club out there, where they were working at.
Dekayla and Dumaine?

I have to kill that Dumaine right on the corner. I forget the name of that club. But we were working out towards the next street down in St. Louis. St. Philip. We were working there close to St. Philip Street.
Where was Mama's?
Mama was right next to us.
Papa? Papa.
Kingfish?
Kingfish.
That's where they were working at, Kingfish. All right. Kingfish.
I live two blocks from there, but I can't keep it straight because it's all changed.
Yeah.
I was there this morning, right?
I think they got a supply of business, all they call it.
They have an arch out there. Yeah. How do you talk about playing sweet and hot and rock and all these different chords?

Well I love to play sweet chords to me. I like to play some nice numbers, not too fast. But in our style, when we play it out, you got to play some nice numbers. You got to play them fast. Of course, you're going to pick one too fast. But you can't get nothing out of them. You play it too fast, you're going to get no understanding. You can't do what you want with your instrument. In fact, I see a sweet fellow, not so awful numbers. You know what I'm talking about. I know you're talking about it. Yeah. . . . I'm working with a rock band. That's some experience for me. Oh boy, it's so bad.
We only got a few more minutes if you can make it. I'll make it. Looks like about seven, five minutes, something like that. You mentioned something about Al Hurd. How did that work?

That was nice, man. I enjoyed winning Chucks with him. He was all right, man. He's a pretty good fella, too. It was really something that I enjoyed. When we were going on the road with him, he would come on stage with his group. Then after they grew, then we would come on with a small band, a seven-piece band. Then after we get off the stage, then Contra would come on with a small seven-piece band. Then Hoist, he would come back and when the ending of the show, he would pick up Clothes of Walker Peek and Divi Ramblin. Then one band would come in, big brass band would come in, one on his side and one on that side. Then they'd march all in together until we get to the bandstand. You understand, we all joined together. Then he would close with the Saints. And Ed O. Emma Thomas, when she was singing with the Contra, and every way he went, he made a hit with it. Some of us had gone to Nevada one time, Reno, but the deal fell true. They'd take the whole thirty-six positions to make that. But I don't know, the deal fell true.
Which band were you with?
With Marty. You were with Marty.
And he had a seven-piece band like a dancer?

We'd take seven out of the brass band. Oh, I see. So he'd pick seven out of the brass band. Al would tell you who we'd pick out the brass band. And we'd take seven out of each band, and make a short band. Then at the end, we'd all get together and play together.
What did Morgan play then?

But when we used a small band he would play clarinet also. But in a big band he'd play clarinet. But the sad part, one trip I think we went to play one night in May, St. George, and the next night we played in Atlanta. Well, how of them had gigs here they couldn't make that. They said, well, I was caught up. He said, how of them over there? Boy, I always said, no, never no more. Never no more. He'd want them back no more. That was nice to work with them, man.
I wonder why he didn't like them.

They couldn't play for her and go out and sing. She always did her sing with Contra. Blast off us. She thought maybe she'd sing with them. If she did better, she sang with us. But if she'd sing with us, she'd sing with Howard. And they couldn't play our numbers. And Albert Walters was with us. He had to go join them to get the band on the right foot.
Did you hear him play piano much by the way? Oh, yeah.

Yeah, I worked with him. Him and I were working in that club back in West End. Used to have nightclubs in West End? With the same Paul Moore. I'll tell you what. Albert was. That's where I first met Albert. He was on piano and I was on band. He worked with Paul Moore, his band back then. Back then. First time I met Albert. And he was a good piano player. He still is good, but you don't have no piano with a voice on. He was a wonderful piano player. Yeah, I hardly ever heard him play piano. He was good. Way back then. When I first came to town I'd hear him different jobs.
Like the one they called the Blue Angel now. Oh, yeah, yeah.
From Peace Fountains. Right along in there.
Somewhere along in there. It was a joint where he played piano. But in late years I just haven't heard him play piano. I thought he was, you know. No, he don't bother with it anymore.
Yeah.

But you know, if Morgan was playing with his brass band he could double on piano. That's right. Just like Picks can double. Well, we used to go to, when we were playing at the Hop Club in Morgan City, we had a band

and Tomless Jefferson playing trumpet where one would get off quick playing piano and Tomless Jefferson would get back on horn and Al would get on piano. Yeah, I've never heard Jefferson play the album.
He's good, too. Everyone says he's very good. He's good. So you didn't have many favorite banjo players?

My favorite banjo player was a guy they called Camphrey. I was going to school and he was playing with Manuel Perez up on the roof guard. He used to have a roof guard in temples. And he was playing there. He was a great banjo player. That was my favorite. So then you got that fellow that died, Peabody, he was great. And the cat I told you was Morris, Nathan Morris, he was another good man. Camphrey died, didn't he? He died in Texas.
He made a record on the map.
I have it on the paper. I'll play it for you something. He was great.
Did you know his brother Percy? Percy Darence, certainly. He played banjo too, but I don't know if he was as good as Caffrey. Tell me more about that WPA and ERA band.

That was a pretty good band. There was nothing to it, though. The only thing you'd go in the morning and rehearse about two hours and you was off the rest of the day. Unless they had a concert before you would go play somewhere. You'd go play a concert in the afternoon or concert at night. Well, I was working in the quarters then. When I was in WPA and then working in the quarters.
Well, that wasn't too hard, I guess. You only worked two hours a day. That's all.
Two hours a day.
Where did you play concerts? Different parts.

We'd go to Shakespeare Park. We'd go up to the hospital, Lester and Hospital, out there in Jackson Square. Sometimes I'd write on Claremont Avenue, Claremont St. Philip, write on the news of the house.
Oh, that used to be beautiful there. Yeah, it was. Those trees and everything. It was nice.
We had to pitch back. Lewis DeMaine was the director of the man during that time. Lewis DeMaine. We were talking here, man. Lewis DeMaine.
Yeah, I never did meet him.
He was the director of the man. And every old guy used to live around here, pitch back, too. I know he was a member of him.
I've heard of him. Yeah.

What did he do? Used to play a metal phone. My every musician Ronnie was in the WPB band during that time. Wasn't nothing else but playing in the band. Get $19 every two weeks. You could live there, off $19.
That's like $10 a week. That's right. And raise your family, bring up your family? That's right.

They used to pick another thing. They picked so many musicians, they had three bands. They had number one, number two, number three bands. They would say you would play the dancers. Like the school, that's some high school, you would go there and play the dancers. Number one band was a big band, or it was about 14 pieces of that. Number two band was a ten piece band. Number three was a seven piece band. I was in that group. Chris Cliff was on trumpet. I can't take the rest of the music. Well, it's just as well with that you don't know how to take.

And I know you're tired. We should appreciate your help, though. So, let me get out a piece of paper for you to sign, if you don't mind. You know, it's easy. Give us the right case somebody wants to write up something in a magazine about you. You got the heavy rule.
I got it, yeah.
And I'll let you read it over before you sign it. Okay. Let's get it.
